title: Multi-Table DI Sets
tagline: Year 3 — Two or three linked tables: combining rows and columns across tables to answer questions

introduction.overview: A multi-table set gives two or three tables that describe the same entities (schools, branches, products) from different angles. Each question usually needs a number from one table and a number from another, combined by multiplication, division or addition. The main task is to identify which tables and which cells a question needs and to combine them with the correct operation.
introduction.placementRelevance: Multi-table sets are a staple of DI sections in company tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Combining a staffing table with a salary table, or enrolment with pass rates, is routine in reports.

learningObjectives: Combine counts and percentages to get new counts
Compute totals, averages and ratios from derived values

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Count = percentage × base ÷ 100; revenue = number × rate. Always check the unit of each table.

coreDefinitions: Linked tables: tables that share rows or columns.
Derived value: number computed from cells in different tables.
Aggregate: a total or average over entities.
Base: the quantity a percentage refers to.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The tables are columns of a single big table split for printing. Rebuild the big table mentally by matching on the common row labels.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: For each question, say which quantities are needed (for example students and pass %), find them in the tables, and combine them with the right operation.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Average of rates
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Not the plain average of percentages

mainNarrative: Table 1 gives students (200, 250, 300, 150, 400), Table 2 gives pass percentages (80, 72, 60, 76, 55) and Table 3 gives the annual fee (₹1,200, ₹1,500, ₹1,000, ₹1,800, ₹900). The number who passed in S3 is 300 × 60% = 180; in S4 it is 150 × 76% = 114.

To find the overall pass percentage, add the passes (160 + 180 + 180 + 114 + 220 = 854) and divide by the total number of students (1,300): about 65.7%. The plain average of the five percentages (68.6%) is wrong because the schools have different sizes.
Fee revenue for a school is students × fee: S2 gives 250 × 1,500 = ₹3,75,000. The total over all schools is the sum of these products.
Comparisons across schools need derived values. The school with the highest number of failures is found by computing students − passed for each.
Always check that a quantity from one table is paired with the right school in another.

deepDiveAspects.title: Weighted vs simple average
deepDiveAspects.content: The overall pass percentage weights each school's percentage by its number of students.

deepDiveAspects.title: Units
deepDiveAspects.content: Never add a count and a percentage; convert first.

solvedExamples.title: Combining two tables
solvedExamples.question: Table 1: S3 has 300 students. Table 2: S3 pass percentage is 60%. How many students of S3 passed?

solvedExamples.title: Revenue
solvedExamples.question: S2 has 250 students and charges ₹1,500 a year per student. What is the annual fee revenue?

steps.title: Pick the cells
steps.explanation: Students 250 from Table 1 and fee ₹1,500 from Table 3.

solvedExamples.title: Overall rate
solvedExamples.question: Five schools together had 854 passes among 1,300 students. What is the overall pass percentage?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Do not average the five percentages.

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Hunt for numbers on each question.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Add derived columns (passed, failed, revenue) once, then answer every question from that extended table.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: A derived count cannot exceed its base.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Add derived columns before reading questions.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Derived values serve many questions in the set.

easy.question:
Table 1: Number of students who appeared in the annual examination

School | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 | S5
Students | 200 | 250 | 300 | 150 | 400

Table 2: Pass percentage

School | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 | S5
Pass % | 80% | 72% | 60% | 76% | 55%

Table 3: Annual fee per student (₹)

School | S1 | S2 | S3 | S4 | S5
Fee (₹) | 1200 | 1500 | 1000 | 1800 | 900

How many students passed in S1?
easy.explanation: S1 passed 80% of 200 = 160. The answer is 160.

The plain average of the five pass percentages is 68.6%. Why is it different from the overall pass percentage?
options: Because the schools have different numbers of students
Because the pass percentages are rounded
Because the tables are in different units
Because the plain average is always higher
placementStyle.correctAnswer: Because the schools have different numbers of students
placementStyle.explanation: The overall rate weights each school by its size (854 ÷ 1,300), so it differs from the plain average of percentages.
